memoryText: For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Ezra 7:10 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is a summary of a whole life. Ezra’s greatness was not in a position but in a heart, and the verse tells us exactly what was in it.

“Ezra had set his heart.” To set the heart is a decision, a firm resolve. It did not happen by accident or by drift. It was a choice made on purpose and kept over time. The Hebrew word means to fix or establish. His heart was anchored.

“To study the Law of the LORD.” The first thing is study. The word means to seek, to inquire, to dig. Ezra approached Scripture as someone who wanted to know it deeply. He was a scribe, skilled in the Law, but skill was not enough. He studied because he loved it.

“And to do it.” The second thing is practice. Knowledge without obedience is empty. Ezra aimed to live what he studied. James 1:22 would later say the same: be doers of the word and not hearers only.

“And to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.” The third thing is teaching. Having studied and obeyed, he shared. His goal was the good of the whole people.

The order here is the pattern for anyone who handles the word of God. You cannot teach what you do not do, and you cannot do what you do not know. If you are a parent, a teacher, a leader in the church, or simply a friend, this verse describes the path. Say it as a prayer: set my heart to study, to do, and to teach.
weekInReview: This week you followed the returned exiles through their first sixty years in the land. You read of the foundation of the temple, the opposition that stopped the work, and the prophets who started it again. You saw the temple finished and the Passover kept with joy. You prayed three psalms of return: Psalm 126, the dream of coming home and the hope of sowing in tears; Psalm 85, the prayer for revival; and Psalm 107, the thanks of those redeemed and gathered from the lands. Then you met Ezra, the scribe who set his heart to study, practice, and teach the law of the LORD. You followed him as he prayed for a safe journey, and as he wept over the sin of the people. The week taught that God keeps his word through the hearts of kings, that opposition cannot stop his work, and that repentance and the word of God are the basis of renewal.
reflectionQuestions: Ezra studied, practiced, and then taught. Which of the three is hardest for you right now, and what is one step you could take?
When the work stopped, God sent prophets to encourage the builders. Who has encouraged you in a stalled season, and who might you encourage?
Ezra prayed with “we” and not “they.” What would it look like to confess sin on behalf of your church or community?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to set your heart to study his law and to do it.
Thank him for teachers who have taught you.
